hints: Notice the starting condition in the diagram: gap width is equal to $\lambda$, which gives the very wide circular spreading labelled $\theta$.

Recall how diffraction spreading depends on the ratio of gap width to wavelength: maximum spreading occurs when width is about $\lambda$, and spreading shrinks as width becomes much larger than $\lambda$.
Think about what fixes the wavelength of the emerging water waves: frequency of the source and speed in the same water, neither of which is changed by widening the gap.
walkthrough: Identify the process in the diagram: plane incident wavefronts of spacing $\lambda$ pass through a gap of width $\lambda$ and spread into circular wavefronts of the same spacing $\lambda$ over angle $\theta$. This is diffraction.
State the diffraction rule: the amount of spreading is large when gap width is similar to $\lambda$ and becomes smaller as gap width increases to be much larger than $\lambda$.
Apply the rule to widening the gap: the ratio width to $\lambda$ increases above 1, so the diffracted beam becomes less spread and more forward-directed, meaning $\theta$ decreases.
Check the wavelength: $v = f\lambda$ for water waves. Widening the obstacle does not change the source frequency $f$ or the wave speed $v$ in the same water, so $\lambda$ remains the same.
Combine the two conclusions: $\theta$ decreases and wavelength remains the same. This is option A.

options.A: Wider gap gives less diffraction so $\theta$ decreases, while frequency and speed in the same water keep $\lambda$ unchanged.
options.B: Increasing $\theta$ is opposite to the diffraction rule - a wider gap relative to $\lambda$ produces less spreading, not more.
options.C: The gap width does not set the wave speed or frequency, so $\lambda$ does not decrease when the gap is widened.
options.D: Passing through a wider gap does not change the medium, so the emerging wavelength does not increase and $\theta$ does not stay the same.
